documents.content:
Test Automation SDK is a comprehensive Python-based testing framework designed for automated testing of automotive systems, particularly those developed with dSPACE tools. It provides a seamless interface to the dSPACE XIL API and offers additional utilities to make testing more efficient and intuitive.

Tip

To get started quickly, follow the Quickstart "Run Turnlamp Demo" which walks you through the process of setting up and running your first test.
documents.title: Test Automation SDK

documents.content:
- XIL API Integration: Unified access to the dSPACE XIL API for connecting to various platforms like VEOS, SCALEXIO, and more
- Test Environment Management: Easy setup and configuration of test environments through Python
- Scenario-Based Testing: Support for scenario-driven testing workflows, including parameter variations
- Real-Time Testing: Support for running real-time test scripts using XIL API TargetScripts
- Data Capturing: Powerful tools for capturing and analyzing simulation data
- Pytest Integration: Convenient fixtures and extensions for use with the pytest framework
- Reporting: Integration with Allure for comprehensive test reporting with Plotly examples in provided demo data
- CLI (`dsta`): Generate type stubs for IDE auto-completion, validate test environment YAML files, and export the JSON schema
documents.title: Key Features

documents.content:
This example shows a simple PyTest function that tests a turn-signal circuit (from the Turnlamp demo) and verifies the correct activation of the right turn signal while ensuring the left signal remains off.

```
import time

from dspace.testautomation import Capturing, TestEnvironmentAccess

def test_turnlamp_activation(ta: TestEnvironmentAccess):
    # Arrange
    # Set battery voltage
    ta.vars.BatteryVoltage.value = 12.0

    # Ensure lever is turned OFF
    ta.vars.TurnSignalLever.value = 0

    # Act
    # Start blinking -> Turn right
    with Capturing(
        [ta.vars.TurnSignalLever,
        ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft,
        ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight]
    ) as capture:
        # Turn signal lever to right
        ta.vars.TurnSignalLever.value = 1

        # Wait is not synchronized with simulation!
        time.sleep(3)
        # Turn signal lever off
        ta.vars.TurnSignalLever.value = 0

    # Assert
    # Get captured signals
    signal_front_right =

documents.content:

        time.sleep(3)
        # Turn signal lever off
        ta.vars.TurnSignalLever.value = 0

    # Assert
    # Get captured signals
    signal_front_right = capture[ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight]
    signal_front_left = capture[ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft]

    # Assert that the turnlamp signal changed (by a value of 1) at least once.
    assert signal_front_right.diff().eq(1).any()

    # Assert that the left turn signal was off all the time
    assert signal_front_left.eq(0).all()
```

You have to note the following restrictions related to the software environment when working with the Test Automation SDK.

The Test Automation SDK supports:

- ASAM XIL 2.2.0 standard only.
- TargetScript feature as of dSPACE XIL API .NET on Linux 2025-A and later.
- AURELION 25.2 and later.
- allure (pip) only. The Test Automation SDK currently has a fix dependency to this test result visualization tool.

For installation prerequisites, such as the supported operating systems, refer to Installation.
documents.title: Installation restrictions

documents.content: You have to note some general limitations and limitations of the Test Automation SDK.
documents.title: Limitations

documents.content:
- Only one .NET Runtime can be used at a time.
- The Test Automation SDK and the dSPACE products used for the test, such as dSPACE XIL API .NET, must be installed on the same PC. As an exception, there is the VEOS installation, because you can access VEOS remotely.
documents.title: General Limitations

documents.content:
- The Test Automation SDK has no access to groups, units, conversion tables, and custom properties of the XIL API mapping.
- The Test Automation SDK does not support merging of multiple mapping files. The XIL API mapping used must therefore contain all the required variables.
- Multiport Capturing does not support triggering. Synchronous capturing of multiple ports is not possible.
- Only TargetScripts in dSPACE Real-Time Testing format are supported.
- ECUMPort and ECUCPort from the ASAM XIL API standard are not supported. Instead for accessing ECU variables, you can use the dSPACE-specific ECUPort implementation, which is a simplified combination of ECUMPort and ECUCPort.
documents.title: Limitations of the Test Automation SDK

The Test Automation SDK provides automation capabilities for dSPACE tools but does not directly depend on their installation. This documentation is intended for users of:

- `dSPACE VEOS` - Virtual ECU and Simulation Platform

documents.title: CLI Reference (dsta)

documents.content:
```
dsta [-v | -vv] <subcommand> [options]
```

The `-v` / `-vv` flag must appear before the subcommand name.
documents.title: Invocation

documents.content:
Option Description `-v` Set log level to `INFO`. `-vv` Set log level to `DEBUG`.

By default (no flag), only `WARNING`-level and above messages are printed.
documents.title: Global options

Generate Python type stub files (`.pyi`) for variables defined in a test environment YAML file. Stub files enable IDE auto-completion and type checking for variables accessed via `TestEnvironmentAccess`.

```
dsta generate --testenv <path> [--output <dir>] [--force]
```
documents.title: dsta generate

documents.content: Option Short Required Default Description `--testenv` `-t` Yes — Path to the test environment YAML file. `--output` `-o` No `./stubs` Output directory for generated stub files. `--force` `-f` No — Delete and recreate the existing output directory. Without this flag the command exits with an error if the output directory already exists.
documents.title: Options

documents.content:
Stub files are written under `<output>/dspace/testautomation/testing/`:

- `testenv.pyi`
- `variables.pyi`
documents.title: Output

documents.content:
```
dsta generate --testenv ./testdata/testenv.yaml --output ./stubs --force
```

After generation, configure Pyright (or your IDE) to locate the stubs:

```
# pyproject.toml
[tool.pyright]
stubPath = "./stubs"
```

For a full walkthrough, refer to Code completion.

An integrated development environment (IDE) is a software application that provides comprehensive facilities to programmers for software development. Examples of popular IDEs include Visual Studio Code, Visual Studio, PyCharm, and Eclipse.

For setting up and working with the Test Automation SDK, we recommend using Visual Studio Code (VS Code). It provides an integrated environment for editing, running, and debugging tests and has a rich extension ecosystem.

For a step-by-step guide to getting started with the SDK, refer to the Quick Start Tutorial.

documents.content:
The Test Automation SDK ships a JSON schema that describes the structure of the test environment YAML file. Registering this schema in your editor unlocks auto-completion, inline validation, and hover documentation while editing `testenv*.yaml` files.

Step 1 – Export the schema

Run the following command in your project root to write `testenv_schema.json` to a `schemas/` directory:

```
dsta schema --output ./schemas
```

Step 2 – Register the schema in VS Code

You can specify the path to the schema at the top of each individual YAML file, or you can supply a pattern to apply the schema automatically to matching file patterns.

To specify the schema for an individual file, add the following line to the top of the file and adjust the file path to point to the path of the generated schema:

```
# yaml-language-server: $schema=path/to/testenv_schema.json
```

To configure the YAML extension in Visual Studio Code to select the schema automatically, add a `yaml.schemas` entry to your
documents.title: Register the Test Environment JSON Schema

documents.content:
hema:

```
# yaml-language-server: $schema=path/to/testenv_schema.json
```

To configure the YAML extension in Visual Studio Code to select the schema automatically, add a `yaml.schemas` entry to your `.vscode/settings.json`:

```
{
  "yaml.schemas": {
    "./schemas/testenv_schema.json": ["**/testenv*.yaml", "**/testenv*.yml"]
  }
}
```

Adjust the glob pattern to match the naming convention used in your project. After saving the settings, the YAML extension validates your test environment files against the schema and provides auto-completion for known fields.

PyCharm / other editors

PyCharm and most other editors support JSON Schema mappings in a similar way. Export the schema with `dsta schema` as above, then configure the schema mapping in your editor's JSON Schema settings. Refer to your editor's documentation for the exact steps.
documents.title: Register the Test Environment JSON Schema

To enable test discovery and execution in VS Code, you need to configure Python tests.

Enable pytest: Click the Test Explorer icon (beaker/flask) in the Activity Bar, then click "Configure Python Tests" and select pytest as the test framework.

Configure pytest arguments: Create or update your `.vscode/settings.json` file in your project folder (e.g., `Demos/demo-turnlamp/.vscode/settings.json`) to specify pytest arguments, including SDK-specific arguments.

You can also access this file via View → Command Palette and run Preferences: Open Folder Settings (JSON).

For more information about testing in VS Code, see the VS Code Python testing documentation. To learn more about using the Test Automation SDK with pytest, refer to Test Environment Access.

Example for dSPACE Release 2024-A:

```
{
  "python.testing.pytestEnabled": true,
  "python.testing.pytestArgs": [
    ".",
    "--testenv-config=testdata/24a/testenv_veos.yaml",
    "--alluredir=allure-results"
  ]
}
```
documents.title: Configure Python Tests with pytest

documents.content:
For projects with a standard test environment, you can configure the test environment path in a `pytest.ini` file instead of specifying it in VS Code settings or on the command line. This eliminates the need to repeatedly pass `--testenv-config` and simplifies project setup.

Create or update a `pytest.ini` file in your project root (e.g., `Demos/demo-turnlamp/pytest.ini`):

```
[pytest]
testenv_config = testdata/24a/testenv_veos.yaml
```

With this configuration in place, you can simplify the VS Code settings:

```
{
  "python.testing.pytestEnabled": true,
  "python.testing.pytestArgs": [
    ".",
    "--alluredir=allure-results"
  ]
}
```

Note: If both the `testenv_config` ini option and the `--testenv-config` command-line argument are provided, the command-line argument takes precedence. This allows for project defaults in `pytest.ini` while still enabling overrides for specific test runs.
documents.title: Alternative: Use pytest.ini Configuration

documents.content:
If you want to generate `result.zip` files per test (see Experiment App and result.zip), you can configure the datacontainers folder in `pytest.ini` instead of passing `--datacontainers` on every test run:

```
[pytest]
testenv_config = testdata/24a/testenv_veos.yaml
datacontainers = sdk-results
```

Or in VS Code settings:

```
{
  "python.testing.pytestEnabled": true,
  "python.testing.pytestArgs": [
    ".",
    "--testenv-config=testdata/24a/testenv_veos.yaml",
    "--datacontainers=sdk-results",
    "--alluredir=allure-results"
  ]
}
```

Note: If both the `datacontainers` ini option and the `--datacontainers` command-line argument are provided, the command-line argument takes precedence.
documents.title: Configuring Data Containers

After configuring pytest as described above:

1. Open the Test Explorer: Click the beaker/flask icon in the Activity Bar (left sidebar) or use View → Testing
2. Discover Tests: VS Code will automatically discover tests in the `tests` directory
3. Run Tests: Click the play button next to individual tests, test classes, or the entire test suite
4. View Results: Test results appear in the Test Explorer panel and inline in the editor

- Test Results: After running tests, click the Show Output button on the right side of the Test Explorer to view detailed test results, including pass/fail status, execution time, error messages, and captured output.

When working with the Test Automation SDK in your IDE or within a continuous integration (CI) environment, you may want to view detailed log messages during test execution. By default, pytest captures and buffers output, which can make real-time logs less visible. However, this behavior can be configured to provide live logging output.

To enable live logging, you can configure pytest using either:

- A `pytest.ini` file
- The `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` block in a `pyproject.toml` file

For example, the following configuration enables live logging and sets the log level to INFO:

```
[pytest]
log_cli = true
log_cli_level = INFO
```

You can also combine this with the test environment configuration:

```
[pytest]
testenv_config = testdata/24a/testenv_veos.yaml
log_cli = true
log_cli_level = INFO
```

Note that this configuration affects pytest’s logging system, not standard output (stdout). Calls to print() will still behave as usual.

Although these settings were originally

documents.content: The Test Automation SDK supports Allure for test report generation. The Allure integration is automatically configured when using pytest with the `dspace-testautomation[pytest]` extra through the `allure-pytest` plug-in, which is installed as a dependency.
documents.title: Reporting

documents.content:
For generating and viewing reports, you need to install the Allure command-line tool:

1. Install Allure following the official documentation.
2. Verify installation by running `allure --version` in your terminal.
documents.title: Installing Allure

documents.content:
Allure is a powerful and flexible test reporting framework that allows you to enrich your test cases with attachments — additional content that provides deeper insight into test behavior. These attachments can include:

- Screenshots
- Logs and trace files
- Text documents
- JSON or XML data
- Static images (e.g., PNG plots)
- HTML content, such as interactive charts and dashboards

One of Allure’s standout features is its ability to embed rich, interactive content directly into the report. This makes it especially useful for visualizing complex test data using plotting libraries such as:

- Plotly – for interactive HTML plots with zoom, pan, and tooltips
- Matplotlib – for static image-based plots
- Bokeh – for web-based interactive visualizations
- Altair, Seaborn, and others – depending on your needs and preferences

By attaching these plots to your test cases and generating the report with `allure generate`, you create a self-contained HTML report that includes all visualizations,
documents.title: Allure Attachments and Embedded Visualizations

documents.content:
g on your needs and preferences

By attaching these plots to your test cases and generating the report with `allure generate`, you create a self-contained HTML report that includes all visualizations, making it easy to review and share test insights.
documents.title: Allure Attachments and Embedded Visualizations

documents.content:
Plotly is a powerful Python library for creating interactive, browser-based visualizations. It allows users to build dynamic plots with features like zooming, panning, tooltips, and legend toggling. In the context of automated testing, Plotly is used to visualize measurement data directly within the Allure test report, making it easier to inspect signal behavior and test outcomes without external tools.

⚠️ When visualizing complex measurement data with Plotly, the resulting plots can become quite large and resource-intensive. This might affect performance, especially in web-based environments or when rendering multiple plots simultaneously.

⚠️ When generating multiple plots, the inline JavaScript components of Plotly can become redundant and significantly increase the output size. To optimize this, consider referencing the standalone `plotly.min.js` library directly. You can find it in your virtual environment under `.../.venv/Lib/site-packages/plotly/package_data/`.

documents.content:
Code completion is a feature in modern IDEs like VS Code or PyCharm that provides the following:

- Auto-completion for variables, methods, and classes
- Tooltips with documentation
- Type checking to catch errors early

When working with dynamically generated or external data like test environment variables code completion might not work out of the box. This is where the type stub files (.pyi) come in.

In order to enable code completion and type hints for test environment variables in your IDE, we provide a script that generates Python type stub files. By using the provided CLI, you can create stubs for seamless auto-completion and improved developer experience when working with the `TestEnvironmentAccess` class. With properly configured stub files, your IDE will offer accurate suggestions, documentation tooltips, and type checking. The script parses the `test environment configuration file` and creates `.pyi` stub files that provide proper type hints for variables accessible via
documents.title: Overview

documents.content: stions, documentation tooltips, and type checking. The script parses the `test environment configuration file` and creates `.pyi` stub files that provide proper type hints for variables accessible via the `TestEnvironmentAccess` class.
documents.title: Overview

documents.content:
- `--testenv`: Path to the test environment YAML file.
- `--output`: (Optional) Output directory for generated stubs. Default is `./stubs`.
- `--force`: (Optional) Overwrite existing output directory.

For a complete reference of all `dsta` subcommands and global options, refer to the CLI Reference.

👉 The following example uses the turnlamp demo from release 24a. To begin, navigate to the `Demos/demo-turnlamp` directory of the Test Automation SDK.

This folder contains the demo project used to run stub generation.

If needed, you can regenerate them using the CLI tool provided by the Test Automation SDK.

Generated stub files are intended for IDE code completion and type checking, not for manual editing or linting. documents.content: This chapter extends the Tutorial by providing a complete overview of signal capturing in the Test Automation SDK and explains the concept behind it.
documents.title: Capturing

documents.content:
The capturing in the Test Automation SDK allows you to capture variable values over time and retrieve them as `pandas` data structures for analysis and validation. It is a powerful mechanism for recording and analyzing signal data during test execution. We fundamentally differentiate between a `Capturing` class for measurements on one port and a `MultiPortCapturing` class for measurements at multiple ports.

Limitation: The Test Automation SDK supports capturing of scalar, vector and matrix variable values. Curve and map values are currently not supported.
documents.title: Capturing Feature Overview

documents.content: The `Capturing` class handles the recording of specified variables during test execution. It works with variables from a single port and provides sophisticated trigger mechanisms.
documents.title: Capturing Class

documents.content: Basic Usage
documents.title: Basic Usage

documents.content: The `Capturing` class functionality can be used with Python's context manager protocol (`with` statement), ensuring proper resource management and automatic cleanup. We recommend this approach. However, it is also possible to call the methods of this class individually, see Manual Usage.
documents.title: Context Manager Pattern

documents.content:
```
import time
from dspace.testautomation import Capturing, TestEnvironmentAccess

def test_signal_capture(ta: TestEnvironmentAccess):
    ta.vars.TurnSignalLever = constants.TURNSIGNAL_LEVER.OFF  # value: 0
    # Configure basic capturing of three signals from same port
    with Capturing([
        ta.vars.TurnSignalLever,
        ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft,
        ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight],
        raster_period=0.01) as capture:
            # Body: Perform test actions after capturing is started
            ta.vars.TurnSignalLever = constants.TURNSIGNAL_LEVER.RIGHT # value: 1
            time.sleep(1.0)
            ta.vars.TurnSignalLever = constants.TURNSIGNAL_LEVER.OFF # value: 0
    # Access captured data from one signal as Pandas.Series object
    left_signal = capture[ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft]
    right_signal = capture[ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight]

    # Access all captured data as Pandas.DataFrame object
    capture_result_frame = capture.get_data_frame()
```
documents.title: Simple Capturing Example

documents.content: In the `test_signal_capture` test example, a `capture` context manager is created that records the signals from the indicator lever and the two front indicators. When the context body is called, the test framework has already initialized and started the capture. When entering the context body, the capture has already been initialized and started by the test framework. Actions to be performed during the ongoing measurement can be defined in the context body. In this example, the indicator lever is switched to the right, a delay of one second is observed, and then the indicator lever is switched off again. When exiting the context body, the measurement is stopped by the test framework. The measured signals can then be retrieved from the `capture` object.
documents.title: Description

documents.content:
The `Capturing` context manager requires the specification of a measurement raster that determines which model task samples the configured variables over time. All specified variables are recorded with that defined raster. Provide exactly one of the following parameters:

- `raster_name`: Selects a measurement raster by its exact name.
- `raster_period`: Selects a periodical raster by its sampling period in seconds. The value must be positive.

Providing either no parameter or both parameters simultaneously raises a `ValueError`.

The concrete raster selection is delegated to port-specific `AbstractCapture` implementations, which apply the following rules.
documents.title: Defining the Measurement Raster

documents.content:
Use `raster_name` to select a specific measurement raster by its exact name. The name must match the raster exactly.

Event-driven and change-driven rasters can only be selected by `raster_name`.

If no raster with that exact name is found, a `CaptureError` is raised.

```
with Capturing(
    [ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft, ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight],
    raster_name="Task_10ms",
    ):
    ...
```
documents.title: Selecting a raster by name

documents.content:
Use `raster_period` to select a periodical raster by its sampling period in seconds. Non-periodical rasters, such as event-driven or change-driven rasters, cannot be selected this way.

- If an exact match exists, that raster is selected.
- If no exact match exists, the next shorter periodical raster is selected and a warning is issued.
- If the requested period is shorter than any available periodical raster, a `CaptureError` is raised.

```
with Capturing(
    [ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft, ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight],
    raster_period=0.001,  # a millisecond periodical raster
    ):
    ...
```
documents.title: Selecting a raster by sampling period

documents.content:
Start and Stop Triggers

You can define conditions that automatically start and stop the capturing process:

```
with Capturing(
    [ta.vars.TurnSignalLever, ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft, ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight],
    raster_period=0.001,
    start_trigger="TurnSignalLever > 0.5",
    stop_trigger="TurnSignalLever < 0.5",
) as capture:
    # Capture is active and waiting for start trigger event to occur.
    ...

    # Switching the lever to the right side will raise the start capture event
    ta.vars.TurnSignalLever = constants.TURNSIGNAL_LEVER.RIGHT  # value: 1

    ...

    # When measurement is running switch the lever off will stop the capturing
    ta.vars.TurnSignalLever = constants.TURNSIGNAL_LEVER.OFF  # value: 0

    ...
```

Triggers with Delays

You can add time delays to triggers by specifying them as tuples after the condition term. Only data acquired between the start trigger time minus a negative delay or plus a positive delay and the stop trigger time plus a
documents.title: Working with Triggers

documents.content:
ys to triggers by specifying them as tuples after the condition term. Only data acquired between the start trigger time minus a negative delay or plus a positive delay and the stop trigger time plus a positive delay is copied to the captured data. If no time delay is specified, the capturing starts and ends exactly at the trigger times.

```
with Capturing(
    [ta.vars.TurnSignalLever, ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft, ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight],
    # Start 0.5s before condition fulfilled
    start_trigger=("BatteryVoltage > 0.5", -0.5),
    # Stop 0.5s after condition fulfilled
    stop_trigger=("TurnSignalLever < 0.05", 0.5),
) as capture:
    ...
```

General notes for triggering

- If the start trigger is never satisfied, the capture remains in ACTIVATED state and no data is recorded. By default, this raises a `CaptureError` (see Handling Unsatisfied Start Triggers and State Model).
- Trigger conditions are port-specific and must follow the syntax supported by the underlying port.
documents.title: Working with Triggers

documents.content:
By default, this raises a `CaptureError` (see Handling Unsatisfied Start Triggers and State Model).
- Trigger conditions are port-specific and must follow the syntax supported by the underlying port.
- Delays are useful to include signal context before/after the trigger event.
documents.title: Working with Triggers

documents.content:
The `require_recording` parameter controls what happens if `start_trigger` is defined but never satisfied. If no `start_trigger` is specified, capturing starts immediately and `require_recording` has no effect.

Default Behavior (require\_recording=True)

When `start_trigger` is defined but not satisfied, a `CaptureError` is raised by default:

```
# This will raise CaptureError if BatteryVoltage never reaches 10000
with Capturing(
    [ta.vars.TurnSignalLever],
    start_trigger="BatteryVoltage == 10000",
    require_recording=True,  # default
) as capture:
    # If trigger never satisfied, CaptureError raised here
    pass
```

Thanks to this default behavior, following code can operate under the assumption that a recorded time series exists. A violation of this assumption is made obvious.

Optional Recording (require\_recording=False)

If you expect the start trigger to not be satisfied and do not want to handle the exception, set `require_recording` to false:

```
# This will only
documents.title: Handling Unsatisfied Start Triggers

documents.content:
us.

Optional Recording (require\_recording=False)

If you expect the start trigger to not be satisfied and do not want to handle the exception, set `require_recording` to false:

```
# This will only log a debug message if trigger not satisfied
with Capturing([ta.vars.TurnSignalLever], start_trigger="BatteryVoltage == 10000", require_recording=False) as capture:
    # No exception raised, only debug log emitted
    pass
```

When the `start_trigger` is not satisfied, no data is recorded and accessing captured signals returns empty objects.
documents.title: Handling Unsatisfied Start Triggers

documents.content:
You can capture the measured data into an ASAM MDF storage file:

```
with Capturing(
    [ta.vars.TurnSignalLever, ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft, ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight],
    datafile_path=pathlib.Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "capture_data.mf4",
) as capture:
    # Test execution
    pass
```

For details of all supported methods, refer to the Capturing class reference.
documents.title: Capture to Data File

documents.content:
The capturing process follows a finite state machine:

States

- CREATED: Capture object instantiated
- ACTIVATED: Waiting for `start_trigger`
- RUNNING: Actively recording
- STOPPED: Recording stopped
- RELEASED: Resources released

Transitions using context manager

From To Condition (with context) CREATED RUNNING enter context without trigger CREATED ACTIVATED enter context with trigger ACTIVATED RUNNING in context after trigger condition met RUNNING STOPPED leave context STOPPED RELEASED leave context Any RELEASED Exception during setup/teardown
documents.title: State Model

documents.content:
Captured signals are returned as pandas Series or DataFrames, depending on the access method:

`get_signal(variable)` → `pandas.Series` After capturing, you can retrieve signals as pandas Series:

```
# Using bracket notation
signal_data = capture[ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft]

# Using get_signal method
signal_data = capture.get_signal(ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft)

print(signal_data.head())
```

Output:

```
0.00    0
0.10    1
0.20    0
0.30    1
0.40    0
```

`get_data_frame()` → `pandas.DataFrame` Aggregates all captured signals into a single DataFrame.

```
# Get all signals as DataFrame
df = capture.get_data_frame()
print(df.head())
```

Output:

```
Time    TurnSignalLever  TurnSignalFrontLeft  TurnSignalFrontRight
0.00    0                0                    0
0.10    1                1                    1
...
```

- Index: Time axis (float, in seconds)
- Columns: Signal names
documents.title: Data Retrieval and Analysis

documents.content:
The `MultiPortCapturing` class handles the recording of specified variables on different ports. In contrast to Capturing, neither start nor stop triggers can be defined. In principle, all variables are sorted according to their port and grouped into a port-specific capture. These are then started sequentially before entering the context or stopped when leaving it.

Note: The created port-specific capture objects are not synchronized.

```
from dspace.testautomation import MultiPortCapturing

with MultiPortCapturing(
    [ta.vars.VariableFromPort1, ta.vars.VariableFromPort2],
    raster_period=0.001,
) as multi_capture:
    # Test execution
    pass

# Access to all signal measurement data for a single port
data_frames_by_port = multi_capture.get_data_frames_by_port()

# Access all measured signals from the available capture items as one single pandas DataFrame
all_signals = multi_capture.get_data_frame()
```

For details of all supported methods, refer to the MultiPortCapturing class
documents.title: Multiport Capturing

documents.content:
ed signals from the available capture items as one single pandas DataFrame
all_signals = multi_capture.get_data_frame()
```

For details of all supported methods, refer to the MultiPortCapturing class reference.
documents.title: Multiport Capturing

documents.content:
- Even if exceptions occur during a port-specific measurement, the measurements on other ports are terminated cleanly.
- Missing values: Filled with `NaN` if signals are not aligned.
documents.title: Notes for Multiport Triggering

documents.content:
Variable Selection

- Only capture variables you actually need for analysis.
- Group related variables in the same capture context.
- Consider the sampling rate and data volume.

Trigger Usage

- Use triggers to capture specific events or time windows.
- Test trigger conditions before implementing them in tests.
- Consider port-specific trigger syntax differences.

Data Analysis

- Leverage pandas functionality for signal analysis.
- Use `.diff()` to detect signal changes.
- Apply `.any()` and `.all()` for boolean checks.
- Extract time stamps using `.index` for time-based analysis.

Resource Management

- Always use the context manager pattern.
- The system automatically handles cleanup and resource release.
- Be aware that empty signals might result if triggers aren't satisfied.
documents.title: Best Practices

documents.content:
Here is a comprehensive example combining all concepts:

```
import time
from dspace.testautomation import Capturing, TestEnvironmentAccess

def test_turn_signal_complete(ta: TestEnvironmentAccess):
    # Arrange - Set initial conditions
    ta.vars.BatteryVoltage.value = 12.0
    ta.vars.TurnSignalLever.value = 0

    # Act - Perform capturing with triggers
    with Capturing(
        [ta.vars.BatteryVoltage, ta.vars.TurnSignalLever, ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight],
        start_trigger="TurnSignalLever > 0.5",
        stop_trigger="TurnSignalLever < 0.1",
    ) as capture:
        # Turn signal lever to right
        ta.vars.TurnSignalLever.value = 1
        time.sleep(3)
        # Turn signal lever off
        ta.vars.TurnSignalLever.value = 0

    # Assert - Evaluate captured data
    front_right_sig = capture.get_signal(ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight)

    # Check for signal changes
    time_stamps_right = front_right_sig[(front_right_sig.diff() == 1)].index
    assert not
documents.title: Complete Example

documents.content:
data
    front_right_sig = capture.get_signal(ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight)

    # Check for signal changes
    time_stamps_right = front_right_sig[(front_right_sig.diff() == 1)].index
    assert not time_stamps_right.empty, "Right signal should have activated"

    # Verify signal states
    assert (front_right_sig == 1).any(), "Signal should be ON at some point"
    assert (front_right_sig == 0).any(), "Signal should be OFF at some point"
```

Summary

The `Capturing` and `MultiPortCapturing` context managers offer robust and flexible mechanisms for signal acquisition in automated XIL API tests. Their integration with pandas enables powerful post-processing and validation workflows.
documents.title: Complete Example

documents.content: In addition to the context manager (`with Capturing(...) as capture:`), the capturing functionality can be used manually. This allows fine-grained control over the lifecycle of the capture object.
documents.title: Manual Usage

documents.content:
```
capture = Capturing([
    ta.vars.TurnSignalLever,
    ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight,
    ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft,
])

capture.start()

# Perform test actions
...

capture.stop()

# Access captured data
signal = capture.get_signal(ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight)
...

capture.release()
```

Transitions using manual usage (without context manager)

From To Condition CREATED RUNNING `start()` without trigger CREATED ACTIVATED `start()` with trigger ACTIVATED RUNNING Trigger condition met RUNNING STOPPED `stop()` or `stop_trigger` met STOPPED RELEASED `release()` Any RELEASED Exception during setup/teardown

Advantages

- Dynamic trigger configuration.
- Full control over start/stop timing.
- Integration with external state machines or test frameworks.

Comparison

Aspect Context Manager (`with`) Manual Usage Lifecycle Automatic Manual Error Handling Built-in (try/finally) Must be implemented manually Resource Cleanup Automatic Requires `release()` call Flexibility Limited to block
documents.title: Example

documents.content:
er (`with`) Manual Usage Lifecycle Automatic Manual Error Handling Built-in (try/finally) Must be implemented manually Resource Cleanup Automatic Requires `release()` call Flexibility Limited to block scope Fully controllable

Error Handling

```
capture = Capturing([...])
try:
    capture.start()
    # Test actions
    ...
    capture.stop()
except Exception as e:
    print("Error during capture:", e)
finally:
    capture.release()
```

Notes

- `start()` must be called before `stop()`.
- Omitting `release()` may lead to resource leaks.
- Trigger conditions can be passed to the constructor but are optional.

Summary

Manual usage of the Capturing class provides maximum flexibility for advanced test scenarios. It requires explicit lifecycle management and careful error handling.
documents.title: Example

documents.content: This chapter provides a conceptual view on configuring and loading the .NET Runtime in the `dspace.testautomation` Pytest-based Test Automation SDK. It focuses on runtime configuration aspects.
documents.title: .NET Runtime Configuration

documents.content:
The configuration allows the .NET Runtime to be loaded on demand, based on the test environment definition. This deferred loading ensures that the runtime is only initialized once the correct context is known, avoiding premature or incorrect initialization.

Deferred loading of the .NET Runtime allows flexibility in choosing between .NET Core (CoreCLR) and .NET Framework at runtime. This is essential for scenarios where different test environments require different runtimes.

The configuration is defined in the `dotnet` section of the test environment YAML file and follows a schema that includes runtime selection, configuration file paths, and search directories for assemblies.
documents.title: Purpose and Design

documents.content: Configuration Options
documents.title: Configuration Options

documents.content:
Specifies the .NET Runtime to use. Supported values:

- `coreclr` – for .NET Core / .NET 5+
- `netfx` – for classic .NET Framework (Windows only)

This setting determines which runtime will be initialized and how assemblies will be loaded.
documents.title: runtime

documents.content:
Path to a `.runtimeconfig.json` file that defines the runtime version and options. It is required when using `coreclr` and can be relative or absolute. See also documentation of pythonnet and .NET Runtime configuration settings

For .NET Core (CoreCLR), the runtime\_config\_file is mandatory because it defines the following:

- The target .NET Runtime version
- Garbage collection and JIT settings
- Assembly binding behavior

Without this file, the CoreCLR host cannot initialize correctly.
documents.title: runtime_config_file

documents.content: A list of directories to search for .NET assemblies. These paths are added to Python’s `sys.path`, allowing dynamic loading of assemblies from these locations.
documents.title: search_paths

documents.content: Example Configurations
documents.title: Example Configurations

documents.content:
```
# test environemnt YAML
dotnet:
  runtime: coreclr
  runtime_config_file: dotnet8.runtimeconfig.json
  search_paths:
    - /opt/dspace/xilapi2024a/Testbench/Main/bin
```

If dSPACE XIL API ports are used in the test environment YAML, the path to the binaries of installation have to be provided in the search paths.
documents.title: Example 1: Using .NET Core with a specific configuration file (dSPACE 24-A, Linux)

documents.content:
```
# test environemnt YAML
dotnet:
  runtime: netfx
```

On Windows with dSPACE Release 24-A or earlier, the .NET Framework has to be selected as runtime. Since the global assembly cache (GAC) is used in that case, it is not necessary to specify `search_paths` for the dSPACE XIL API. Since `netfx` is also the default setting in Windows, the dotnet configuration can be omitted entirely.
documents.title: Example 2: Using .NET Framework with default settings (dSPACE 24-A, Windows)

The following table lists required .NET Runtimes for dSPACE XIL API Releases and their default installation path.

documents.title: dSPACE Release defaults

documents.content:
If no configuration is provided, the system falls back to platform defaults:

- On Windows: `netfx`
- On Linux/macOS: `coreclr` (with internal default configuration)

A warning is logged to indicate which runtime was selected implicitly.
documents.title: Fallback Behavior

documents.content:
Before applying platform defaults, the system checks for environment variables only if the corresponding settings are not provided in YAML:

Variable Purpose `PYTHONNET_CORECLR_RUNTIME_CONFIG` Path to .runtimeconfig.json for CoreCLR initialization `DOTNET_ROOT` Path to the .NET installation root (where hostfxr resides)

If these variables are set and the YAML does not specify these values, they are considered during runtime configuration.
documents.title: Environment Variable Consideration

documents.content:
Internally, the runtime is initialized via a controlled bootstrap process:

1. The configuration is parsed from the YAML file.
2. The runtime is selected and loaded using the provided settings.
3. Search paths are added to `sys.path`.
4. Assemblies are loaded as needed.
5. Types and instances from .NET assemblies are accessed via `dotnet` module.

This process ensures that the runtime is only loaded once and that all .NET interactions are routed through a dedicated interface.
documents.title: Runtime Initialization Flow

documents.content:
⚠️ User code in tests should not not use the `pythonnet` and `clr` modules directly. The .NET Runtime is loaded once the test environment YAML is read. User code in tests, that need to access .NET assemblies and types, should access these only via the `dotnet` module.

If the user code relies on .NET in a way that cannot be implemented as described above, e.g., due to third-party libraries, access to .NET should be moved to the test methods after the test environment YAML has been loaded. This includes “import” statements for Python modules that access .NET assemblies during import. In any case, different .NET versions must not be mixed, and the .NET assemblies used by the user code and its dependencies must be compatible with the .NET version configured for the test environment.
documents.title: Limitations on User Code

documents.content:
```
from dspace.testautomation.common import dotnet

def test_whatever():
    # Load the named assembly from provided search paths
    dotnet.load_assembly("MyNamespace.MyAssembly")

    # Create an instance of a .NET type using its fully qualified name
    foo = dotnet.get_instance("MyNamespace.MyAssembly.MyType")
    assert foo is not None
```

documents.content: The Test Automation SDK can create isolated `result.zip` files per test, which can be read and displayed by the dSPACE Experiment App.
documents.title: Experiment App and result.zip

documents.content:
When `pytest` is used to run Test Automation SDK tests and the optional command line argument `--datacontainers` is specified to set a root folder for storing local test artifacts, the `dspace-testautomation` pytest plug-in creates a separate result.zip file for each test, containing:

- all captures as .mf4 files.
- a reduced XIL API mapping XML file containing only the variables used in the captures.
- "log.pytest.txt" file, which contains the captured logging from setup, call, and teardown of a the test function.
- "log.dspace.xml" file, which is a export of the dSPACE message log file reduced to the test relevant times and sessions.

The datacontainer folder and the result.zip files are organized as follows:

1. The pytest option `--datacontainers` defines the root folder for all “result.zip” files.
2. For each session, a subfolder is created with the time stamp of the session start.
3. For each concrete test, a subfolder is created with the name of the test method, as defined by
documents.title: result.zip

documents.content:
sult.zip” files.
2. For each session, a subfolder is created with the time stamp of the session start.
3. For each concrete test, a subfolder is created with the name of the test method, as defined by pytest. The file name is cleaned up so that certain characters can be replaced from argument values from concrete test method executions.
4. The result.zip is created in the local folder for each test.

Note that only automatic creation is currently supported. There are plans to offer a feature for programmatically creating such a result.zip file from within a test in the future.

Example

To run tests with pytest and the Test Automation SDK and generate result.zip files per test, you must specify the command line option `--datacontainers` in addition to the mandatory option `--testenv-config`.

The following example searches the current directory (`.`) for test files, runs the tests with the configured test environment, and creates result.zip files that are stored in the `./sdk-results`
documents.title: result.zip

documents.content:
g`.

The following example searches the current directory (`.`) for test files, runs the tests with the configured test environment, and creates result.zip files that are stored in the `./sdk-results` folder. Each pytest session creates a separate folder with the time stamp of the session start, so you do not have to worry about results being overwritten.

```
pytest . --testenv-config=test-environment.yaml --datacontainers=sdk-results
```

Alternative: For a project-specific standard datacontainers folder, you can configure it in `pytest.ini`:

```
[pytest]
datacontainers = sdk-results
```

This eliminates the need to specify `--datacontainers` on the command line for every test run. The command-line argument `--datacontainers` takes precedence over the ini option if both are provided.

documents.content:
Variable mappings decouple test code from environment-specific identifiers. Tests can be expressed against aliases, making them portable across environments by simply remapping aliases.

In general, variable mapping maps a unique short alias (`FrameworkVariable`), to be used in tests, to a specific port and a corresponding port-specific identifier (`PortVariable`), to access the values from the hardware or software resource abstracted by that port.

The variable mapping has to be configured in the test environment configuration YAML file. The registry is populated with the mapping information. The `TestEnvironmentAccess` class and `ta` pytest fixture look up these alias in the registry and delegate read and write access to the associated port with the port-specific identifier. Refer to Variable Access for more information.
documents.title: Variable Mapping - Configuration

documents.content:
Variable mappings must be configured in the test environment configuration YAML file, in the `mappings` section. The `mappings` section is a list of `file` and `type` pairs, where `file` is an absolute or relative (to the YAML file) file path and the `type` property specifies the format of that defined mapping.

The variable mapping can be configured in three different formats.

- `"XIL API Mapping"`: The ASAM XIL API Mapping XML is a standardized XML format.
- `"CSV"`: A simple comma separated values (CSV) file, easier to create from scratch.
- `"ASM"`: A generative approach for SCBT tests, where a variable mapping is created based on a dSPACE Automotive Simulation Model Traffic XML file.

It is possible to define several variable mapping files, even from different sources. The following two constraints exist regardless of format.

1. Framework variables or aliases must be unique in the current test environment across variable mapping files. However, it is possible that a
documents.title: Test Environment YAML

documents.content:
he following two constraints exist regardless of format.

1. Framework variables or aliases must be unique in the current test environment across variable mapping files. However, it is possible that a port-specific variable is mapped to by two different aliases.
2. Port variables must be associated with a port from the test environment YAML. The relation is always resolved by name.

If a port-specific variable is not associated to a port or the aliases are not unique, the setup of the test environment will fail.
documents.title: Test Environment YAML

documents.content:
The preferred way of defining mappings for the Test Automation SDK is the standardized ASAM XIL API Mapping file format. This is currently the most versatile format the Test Automation SDK supports, though some of the information of that format is not used, e.g., mapping groups. If you already have ASAM XIL Mapping files from using other dSPACE programs or if you can generate them, stick to that format.

To create a mapping, refer to our user documentation on the XIL Mapping Tool Chain for HIL or SIL Simulations.

```
# test-environment.yaml
mappings:
  - file: VEOS/turnlamp/Mappings/TurnLampMapping.xml
    type: XIL API Mapping
```
documents.title: ASAM XIL API Mapping XML Files

documents.content: This CSV-based mapping approach serves as a simplified alternative to the ASAM XIL API mapping. Instead of configuring complex mappings through the XIL API, you can provide the necessary information in a straightforward CSV format. This makes it easier to integrate with the test framework and reduces setup complexity.
documents.title: Mapping as Comma-Separated Value File (CSV)

documents.content:
The mapping must be provided as a UTF-8 encoded CSV file.

Following columns are mandatory:

- `"FrameworkLabel"`: Unique name for the variable to be used in test code.
- `"PortId"`: Identifier of the port used to access the corresponding resource. Must match the port name defined in the test environment YAML configuration file (e.g., `Model`).
- `"TestbenchLabel"`: Port‑specific identifier of the model variable on the testbench.
- `"TestbenchType"`: Data type of the test bench variable. The value in the TestbenchType must be a valid NumPy data type, such as float32, int64, or bool. For a complete list of supported types, refer to the official NumPy documentation.
- `"Dimension"`: Optional column to express the number of dimensions of the variable. Valid values are `0` for scalar values, `1` for vectors, and `2` for matrices. If the value or the entire column is omitted, the number of dimensions defaults to `0` (scalar values).

Following columns are supported but not required:

-
documents.title: Required Format

documents.content:
es, `1` for vectors, and `2` for matrices. If the value or the entire column is omitted, the number of dimensions defaults to `0` (scalar values).

Following columns are supported but not required:

- `"IsWritable"`: Defines whether the mapped framework variable can be modified at run time or is read-only. Allowed column entries are true/false, yes/no, positive/negative, and 1/0. If no value is given, the default is true.

Furthermore:

- Additional columns might be present but are ignored.
- The order of columns in the CSV file is flexible. As long as all required column headers are present and the values are correctly assigned to their respective headers, the columns can appear in any order.
- The delimiter used in the CSV file is automatically detected based on the header line.
- All required fields must contain valid, non-empty values.
documents.title: Required Format

documents.content:
```
FrameworkLabel,PortId,TestbenchLabel,TestbenchType,IsWritable
BatteryVoltage,Model,Model Root/BatteryVoltage[V]/Value,float64,true
TurnSignalLever,Model,Model Root/TurnSignalLever[-1..1]/Value,float64,true
```

```
# test-environment.yaml
mappings:
  - file: excel_mapping.csv
    type: CSV
```

The Test Automation SDK provides the option to generate a XIL API Mapping XML file from a specified ASM Traffic XML file. In that case, aliases are defined based on the signal names and metadata extracted from the ASM XML structure, particularly from the `PlotSignals/Collector` section and maneuver control definitions. The generated alias names are sanitized to form valid Python identifiers, so the available aliases have operator symbols such as square brackets replaced by underscores.

Note that the use of this variable mapping option will connect the associated XIL API MAPort (refer to Ports - Lifecycle Operations) to determine the type information of variables, which might have further side effects depending on your configuration.

```
# test-environment.yaml
mappings:
  - file: asmtraffic/VEOS/ASM_Traffic.xml
    type: ASM
```

Using `ASM` as the mapping format creates an ASAM XIL API Mapping file in addition to the ASM Traffic source file with the same name and the suffix
documents.title: ASM Traffic XML File

documents.content:
: asmtraffic/VEOS/ASM_Traffic.xml
    type: ASM
```

Using `ASM` as the mapping format creates an ASAM XIL API Mapping file in addition to the ASM Traffic source file with the same name and the suffix `.xilmapping_generated.xml`.

documents.content:
This chapter explains how to configure ports in the test environment YAML file. It begins with general concepts and then describes each supported port type in detail, based on the current schema.

A port is an abstraction that wraps a third-party component (software or hardware) of the test environment and standardizes its lifecycle (create/connect/start/stop/disconnect/release) and its data access (read/write/capture).

Concrete ports are subclasses of `AbstractPort` and are instantiated from entries in the test environment YAML file. After the YAML file is processed, all ports are instantiated and accessible via `TestEnvironmentAccess`. However, their underlying managed resources are not yet created at this stage. See Ports — Lifecycle & Orchestration
documents.title: Ports — Configuration

documents.content:
Ports are defined as a list under the top-level key `ports`:

```
# test-environment.yaml
ports:
  - type: XIL API MAPort
    name: Model
    order: 10
    target_state: CONNECTED
    config:
      port_config_file: ./cfg/ma_port.xml
      force_config: true
  # ...more ports...
```
documents.title: Definition of Ports in Test Environment YAML

documents.content:
- Name must be unique. The `name` is a free-form string identifier used throughout the test environment (e.g., in mappings). It must be unique among all ports.
- Setup order. The `order` determines the setup/teardown sequence by means of a natural number. Ports with lower numbers are set up earlier, and teardown occurs in reverse order. If multiple ports share the same order, their relative setup order is undefined.
- Target lifecycle state. The `target_state` specifies the state that the setup must reach (`RELEASED`, `CREATED`, `CONNECTED`, `STARTED`). More information about these states can be found in Ports — Lifecycle & Orchestration.
- File path resolution. Any key ending in `file` is resolved to an absolute path relative to the YAML file’s directory (unless it is already absolute).
- Custom ports & plug-ins. If `type:`Custom` is used, the class is detected from a specified folder. See Custom port for details.
- Config flattening. The `config:` object of each port is flattened.
documents.title: General Configuration Aspects

documents.content:
.
- Custom ports & plug-ins. If `type:`Custom` is used, the class is detected from a specified folder. See Custom port for details.
- Config flattening. The `config:` object of each port is flattened. That means that nested dictionaries are converted to dot-separated keys (e.g., `foo: { bar: 1 }` ⇒ `foo.bar: 1`). Lists are not flattened - they remain as lists and are accessible under their original key. However, this is only of interest when providing custom ports or when you need to access the configuration of instantiated ports.
- File path resolution in lists. The file path resolution described above also applies within lists. Any string value whose key ends with `_file` or is exactly `file` is resolved to an absolute path, regardless of whether it appears at the top level of `config`, inside a nested dictionary, or inside a list of objects. This means the following relative file paths will be resolved to absolute paths:

```
config:
  connections:
    - ip: 192.168.140.20
documents.title: General Configuration Aspects

documents.content:
config`, inside a nested dictionary, or inside a list of objects. This means the following relative file paths will be resolved to absolute paths:

```
config:
  connections:
    - ip: 192.168.140.20
      esi_configuration_file: ./ESI_ABC_SignalConfiguration.yaml
    - ip: 192.168.140.30
      esi_configuration_file: ./ESI_ABC_SignalConfiguration.yaml
```

- Validation & Schema. The YAML file is validated against the bundled JSON Schema to ensure consistent and valid configurations. If the provided test environment YAML fails validation, a `ConfigurationError` is raised and the tests are canceled.

To obtain the schema file, run:

```
dsta schema --output ./schemas
```

This writes `testenv_schema.json` to the specified directory. The file is also bundled with the installed package at `dspace/testautomation/data/testenv_schema.json` inside the package installation folder. If you followed the tutorial, the full path to the schema file is:
documents.title: General Configuration Aspects

documents.content:
s also bundled with the installed package at `dspace/testautomation/data/testenv_schema.json` inside the package installation folder. If you followed the tutorial, the full path to the schema file is: `$HOME/TestAutomationSDK/.venv/Lib/site-packages/dspace/testautomation/data/testenv_schema.json`. You can supply this schema to your preferred editor to enable editing support.

Example: Minimal skeleton for any port

```
- type: "<one of the supported types>"
  name: "<unique-port-name>"
  order: <integer>
  target_state: "<RELEASED|CREATED|CONNECTED|STARTED>"
  config:
    # port-specific keys...
```

Example: ControlDesk Port

```

```
documents.title: config keys

documents.content:
The defaults for the config options, except for `project` and `experiment`, are optimized for automated execution in CI/CD pipelines. In such environments, you typically want to reopen the ControlDesk project for each test run and avoid retaining changes when the project is closed at the end of the test.

During interactive test runs, for example, during test development, these default settings can be disruptive, especially when the ControlDesk application is already running and the desired project and experiment are already open. For local, non-intrusive execution, where users might alternate between using the Test Automation SDK and performing manual exploratory work in ControlDesk, we recommend the following settings:

- `make_visible: true`: Ensures that ControlDesk becomes visible when first accessed.
- `reload_project: false`: Prevents reloading of the project if the correct project is already open.
- `save_changes: true`: Saves modifications to an already opened project if it
documents.title: Configuration recommendations for different use cases

documents.content:
when first accessed.
- `reload_project: false`: Prevents reloading of the project if the correct project is already open.
- `save_changes: true`: Saves modifications to an already opened project if it must be closed by the Test Automation SDK in order to load the required project.
- `teardown_actions: none` or `go_offline`: Minimizes disruptions during interactive work in ControlDesk after completing a test run. Be aware that when ControlDesk is online, it prevents other programs from downloading an application.

Example: Interactive Development and Experimenting with ControlDesk

config:
  make_visible: true  # Make visible if hidden; does not actively hide.
  reload_project: false  # Leave an already opened project and experiment as is.
  save_changes: true  # Save modifications to an already opened project.
  teardown_action: none  # Or go_offline, depending on your workflow. For less interference while experimenting interactively.
```

- `class_name` (string, required) — the fully qualified name of the plug-in class to instantiate.
- `config` (object; free‑form) — arbitrary key value pairs that are passed to the plug-in. Note that all nested configuration keys are flattened and file names are resolved as described in General Configuration Aspects. Lists are kept as lists (not flattened), and file path resolution is applied recursively to any string values within list items whose keys end with `_file` or is exactly `file`. If you supply a `null` value, the corresponding key will be discarded.

Example: Custom Port

```
plugins:
  - folder: ./plugins
ports:
  - type: Custom
    class_name: mycompany.ports.SpecialPort
    name: sp
    order: 60
    target_state: CONNECTED
    config:
      endpoint_url: http://localhost:9000
      credentials_file: ./secrets/creds.json
```
documents.title: Port keys

documents.content: This chapter explains how to implement and use a custom port. Use a custom port to integrate systems that are not covered by built-in port types. Typical cases include 3rd-party tools.
documents.title: Ports — Custom Port

documents.content:
A custom port must inherit from `AbstractPort` and implement these lifecycle methods:

- `create()`
- `connect()`
- `start()`
- `stop()`
- `disconnect()`
- `release()`

These methods manage the resource lifecycle in a consistent order called by the framework during test setup and teardown or during test execution.

The custom port implementation must also provide two properties: `state` (read-only), which returns the current `PortState` (`RELEASED`, `CREATED`, `CONNECTED`, or `STARTED`), and `origin` (read-only), which exposes the underlying wrapped resource, if any.

For lifecycle model and operation semantics, refer to Lifecycle States, and Lifecycle Operations.

If state preconditions are violated, raise `PortStateError` with a clear message.
documents.title: Required Interface

documents.content:
All state transition methods can accept optional keyword arguments via `**kwargs`. Use an optional `lifecycle_context` keyword argument to identify call origin.

This enables different behavior when a transition is invoked:

- During framework startup.
- During framework teardown.
- During test execution or user-invoked calls.

This pattern is useful for behaviors such as teardown-specific handling where the port should act differently for framework-invoked transitions than for calls from fixtures or test code.

The allowed values of the argument are defined in `PortLifecycleContext`.
documents.title: Optional lifecycle_context Keyword Argument

documents.content:
Optionally, implement capability interfaces from `ports.capabilities` to expose features like variable read/write, measurement capture, error simulation, or target script execution. Use multiple inheritance so the class extends both `AbstractPort` and the capability interface(s).

For example, `class MyPort(AbstractPort, VariableAccessCapability)` enables variable access workflows.

For capability method requirements, refer to Capabilities.
documents.title: Capabilities

documents.content:
Configuration parameters are passed to the port via the `config` dictionary in the `__init__()` method. Use the helper method `self.get_option(key, raise_error=True)` to safely retrieve required keys with error handling. Optionally, `get_option()` also supports default values. Outside the `__init__()` method, use the property `self.config` to access the port configuration.

In the test environment YAML file, register your port using `type: Custom`, specify the `class_name`, and list the `plugins` folder where your module is saved.

For complete YAML details, refer to Ports — Configuration.
documents.title: Configuration

documents.content:
Once configured and initialized, your port is available through `TestEnvironmentAccess` under `ta.ports.<name>`.

If your port implements `VariableAccessCapability`, framework-level variable read/write operations automatically route through your `read()` and `write()` methods.
documents.title: Usage in Tests

documents.content: This chapter lists and explains the different ports of the Test Automation SDK.
documents.title: Ports — Details

documents.content:
Ports in the Test Automation SDK implement various capability interfaces that define the operations of the port. The main capabilities are:

- `VariableAccessCapability` — Allows reading and writing of variables in the connected tool or system.
- `MeasurementCapability` — Enables data capture and measurement during test execution.
- `ElectricalErrorCapability` — Provides functionality for simulating electrical faults in automotive testing.
- `TargetScriptCapability` — Allows execution of real-time scripts on the target system during testing.

By integrating with dSPACE Failure Insertion Units (FIU), the EESPort allows test engineers to programmatically inject and control electrical errors during test execution, simulating real-world wiring faults such as short circuits, line breaks, and voltage anomalies.

The Test Automation SDK's `XilEesPort` class wraps the XIL API's .NET interface, providing a Python interface that integrates with the pytest-based test framework.

documents.content: The EESPort follows a well-defined lifecycle with specific states. Each state represents a different level of functionality and determines which operations are permitted.
documents.title: Port Lifecycle and States

documents.content: XIL API State TA SDK State Description eDISCONNECTED CREATED Port object created but not connected to hardware. Configuration loading is possible. eCONNECTED CONNECTED Port connected to FIU hardware. Error configuration can be assigned. eDOWNLOADED CONNECTED Error configuration downloaded to hardware. Ready to start simulation. eACTIVATED CONNECTED Error simulation active. System monitors for trigger events.
documents.title: State Definitions

documents.content:
The port progresses through the states via specific method calls:

```
[CREATED] ──create()──> [CREATED]
    │
    └──connect()──> [CONNECTED (eCONNECTED)]
           │
           └──download()──> [CONNECTED (eDOWNLOADED)]
                  │
                  └──activate()──> [CONNECTED (eACTIVATED)]
                         │              │
                         │              └──trigger()──> [Error Injected]
                         │
                         └──deactivate()──> [CONNECTED (eDOWNLOADED)]
                                │
                                └──unload()──> [CONNECTED (eCONNECTED)]
```
documents.title: State Transitions

documents.content:
The `XilEesPort` class provides the following lifecycle management methods:

- `create()` — Creates the EESPort instance using the testbench factory
- `connect()` — Loads port configuration and connects to FIU hardware
- `download(error_config_filepath)` — Downloads error configuration to hardware (optionally loads from file)
- `activate()` — Activates error simulation, system waits for triggers
- `deactivate()` — Deactivates error simulation, returns to Downloaded state
- `unload()`— Unloads error configuration, returns to Connected state
- `trigger()` — Manually triggers the next error in the configured sequence
documents.title: Lifecycle Methods

documents.content: Port configuration files define the connection between the EESPort and the FIU hardware. These XML files specify hardware drivers, signal mappings, and platform-specific settings. Port configuration files use the `.portconfig` extension. Details about the Port Configurations file must be specified in the user documentation of the EESPort manufacturer, as the structure of the XML file is manufacturer-specific.
documents.title: Port Configuration

documents.content: Error configurations define the specific electrical faults to inject during testing. These are separate XML files that specify error sets, signal targets, error types, and trigger modes. Details about an ErrorConfigurations file must be specified in the user documentation of the EESPort manufacturer, as the structure of the XML file is manufacturer-specific.
documents.title: Error Configuration

documents.content:
The EESPort is configured in the test environment YAML file alongside other ports. Refer to XIL API EESPort to see the basic configuration. This configuration is loaded automatically when the test environment is initialized. For more information about defining ports in the test environment YAML, see Definition of Ports in Test Environment YAML.

On certain platforms, the simulation model must be loaded and started before the EESPort can be used. For this purpose, use the XIL API MAPort. This means that, in addition to the EESPort, a MAPort must also be listed in the port section of the configuration file. To ensure that the simulation is loaded before the EESPort is created, you must specify a lower order number for the MAPort than for the EESPort.

documents.content: The Test Automation SDK provides the `ErrorConfiguration` context manager to simplify error simulation in tests. The following is a real example taken from the TA SDK demo tests.

documents.content:
The recommended approach is to use the `ErrorConfiguration` context manager, which automatically handles the complete lifecycle (download, activate, trigger, deactivate, unload). The `ErrorConfiguration` context manager requires the path to the ErrorConfiguration file. If only one EESPort is specified in the test environment YAML file, it is automatically used to load the ErrorConfiguration file. If multiple EESPorts are configured in the test environment YAML file, the name of the desired EESPort must be passed to the `ErrorConfiguration` context manager as a second parameter.

ROOT_DIR = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent

documents.content: This document focuses on the port lifecycle: States, transitions, and how the `TestEnvironmentAccess` and the `ta` pytest fixture control ports during setup and teardown.
documents.title: Ports — Lifecycle & Orchestration

documents.content:
A port is an abstraction over a third-party hardware or software resource. It encompasses connection/start/stop/release and provides a uniform interface so that tests can be performed with a consistent lifecycle, regardless of vendor or product. All ports of the `dspace.testautomation` implement the `AbstractPort` abstract class.

The ports feature two main aspects:

1. A lifecycle model to set up (`create()`, `connect()` and `start()`) and tear down (`stop()`, `disconnect()`, `release()`) managed software products like XIL API MAPort or dSPACE ControlDesk.
2. Access specific parts, properties, or values of the underlying software resource - e.g., reading and writing model variables via the XIL API MAPort or dSPACE ControlDesk.
documents.title: Ports

documents.content:
Ports follow a minimal state model defined in the `PortState` enum:

- `RELEASED` (0): The resource is not yet created or has already been released. For example, the port is specified in test environment YAML, and the `AbstractPort` instance is created, but the underlying software or hardware resource is not yet instantiated.
- `CREATED` (1): The resource is created and accessible via the `origin` property, but is not yet connected or configured. For example, a dSPACE MAPort is instantiated, but is not yet configured to use the specified simulation application or platform.
- `CONNECTED` (2): The resource is fully configured, operable, and ready to use.
- `STARTED` (3): A port-specific substate of `CONNECTED`. This state may not be meaningful for all implementations. For example, an ASAM XIL API MAPort is considered to be`STARTED` if the connected simulation application is running. In contrast, there is no equivalent concept for an ASAM XIL API ECU Port.

Each port exposes a read-only
documents.title: Lifecycle States

documents.content:
XIL API MAPort is considered to be`STARTED` if the connected simulation application is running. In contrast, there is no equivalent concept for an ASAM XIL API ECU Port.

Each port exposes a read-only `state` property that reflects the state of the underlying resource. The concrete vendor instance is exposed via the `origin` read-only property. Accessing origin in the `RELEASED` state raises a `PortStateError` error.
documents.title: Lifecycle States

documents.content:
Every concrete port implements the following methods (semantics can vary depending on implementation):

- `create()` — create the resource. E.g., a XIL API MAPort instance.
- `connect()` — Configure and connect the resource. Ports may require specific configurations, which are provided in the test environment YAML file.
- `start()` — Start the resource. The meaning is heavily dependent on implementation and the resource. This may also be no-op. In that case, the state will stay `CONNECTED`.
- `stop()` — Stop the resource. A stopped port is expected to be startable again. Similar to `start()` this is heavily port-specific.
- `disconnect()` — Disconnect the resource.
- `release()` — Release the resource acquired by `create()`. It is possible to create a new port `origin`resource if `create()` is invoked on a `RELEASED` port.

Note: No implicit state transitions occur. Callers must explicitly manage transitions. If a `STARTED` port should be reconfigured, it is the responsibility of the
documents.title: Lifecycle Operations

documents.content:
()` is invoked on a `RELEASED` port.

Note: No implicit state transitions occur. Callers must explicitly manage transitions. If a `STARTED` port should be reconfigured, it is the responsibility of the caller to `stop()`, `disconnect()`, and `connect()` again with a possibly different configuration.
documents.title: Lifecycle Operations

documents.content:
The `TestEnvironmentAccess` controls the ports during setup to their declared `target_state` and unwinds them during teardown. It operates strictly in the specified `order` (ascending for setup, reverse for teardown).

For each port defined in test environment YAML (in the specified `order`), the `TestEnvironmentAccess` performs an advance to the specified target state. If a setup step fails, an error is logged and the teardown of already processed ports is initiated. Finally a `PortError` which effectively stops test execution is raised.

Errors are logged per port; after attempting all ports, the TestEnvironmentAccess raises a `PortError` if any failures occurred.
documents.title: Orchestration (Setup & Teardown)

documents.title: Scenario-Based Testing

documents.content:
`dspace.testautomation.scenario.Scenario` provides a high-level interface for SDK-based tests to download, initialize, and execute scenarios (defined as the combination of a maneuver XML and a road (.rd) description) and to evaluate their outcomes, while hiding port-specific differences (ModelDesk, AURELION, MAPort) behind a consistent API for parameterization and execution.

Typical flow:

```
from dspace.testautomation.scenario import Scenario

def test_ego_velocity_60(ta: TestEnvironmentAccess) -> None:
    scenario = Scenario(maneuver="maneuver", road="road")
    # Optional parameterization
    scenario.vars.v_EGO.value = 60
    # or
    # scenario.apply_parameters({"v_EGO": 60})
    # Init, then run
    scenario.init()
    with Capturing([ta.vars.v_Total_Vehicle_km_h]) as capture:
        scenario.start()
        scenario.wait_for_maneuver_finished()
    # Optional: If you need explicit stop/end
    # scenario.stop()
```

⚠️ Parameterization after `init()`: Setting scenario
documents.title: Overview

documents.content:
re:
        scenario.start()
        scenario.wait_for_maneuver_finished()
    # Optional: If you need explicit stop/end
    # scenario.stop()
```

⚠️ Parameterization after `init()`: Setting scenario parameters after `init()` can lead to inconsistent behavior and is not recommended. Always set parameters before calling `init()`.
documents.title: Overview

documents.content:
Depending on the available ports in the current test environment, the `Scenario` factory will use one of the following implementations:

- ModelDesk + AURELION → `ModelDeskAurelionScenario`
- ModelDesk only (no AURELION) → `ModelDeskScenario`
- XIL API MAPort (dSPACE) → `ModelDeskMAPortScenario`
  - MAPort config (XML) must already contain the road/scenario XML structure under the `ScenarioApiConfig` element.
documents.title: Scenario Type Selection

documents.content:
You can parameterize scenarios in three ways:

1. Attribute-style variables via `scenario.vars.<name>.value`:

```
scenario.vars.v_EGO.value = 70
scenario.vars.d_Fellow.value = 0.1
```

1. Bulk mapping via `scenario.apply_parameters({ ... })`:

```
scenario.apply_parameters({"v_EGO": 60, "d_Fellow": 0})
```

1. When initializing the scenario via `scenario.init(...)`

```
scenario.init(v_EGO=60, d_Fellow=0)
```
documents.title: Parameter Handling

documents.content:
Lifecycle methods that matter after `init()`:

```
scenario.init()                         # downloads & initializes the scenario
scenario.start()                        # starts execution
scenario.wait_for_maneuver_finished()   # blocks until maneuver finishes
scenario.stop()                         # optional explicit stop
```

ℹ️ Before `init()`, some states/values can be undefined or contain placeholder values. Only after `init()` do lifecycle queries become meaningful.

When validating behavior, synchronize with other test infrastructure (e.g., Capturing) to ensure signal traces cover the full maneuver run.
