breadcrumbs: Real-Time Testing Using ASAM XIL API TargetScripts
documents.content: The targetscript (`dspace.testautomation.targetscript`) Python subpackage provides an easy way to load and start real-time test scripts. It is based on TargetScript from the ASAM XIL API standard. The TargetScript implementation by dSPACE uses Real-Time Testing which is vendor-specific. The `TargetScriptRTT` class simplifies the process of executing dSPACE-specific real-time test scripts on target platforms, handling configuration generation, script loading, execution, and cleanup.
documents.title: Overview

breadcrumbs: Real-Time Testing Using ASAM XIL API TargetScripts
documents.content:
- TargetScripts are limited to MAPorts only.
- The `targetscript` package currently only supports dSPACE real-time scripts.
- TargetScripts are supported on Linux platforms starting with dSPACE Release 2025-A.
documents.title: Limitations

breadcrumbs: Real-Time Testing Using ASAM XIL API TargetScripts
documents.content: Usage Patterns
documents.title: Usage Patterns

breadcrumbs: Real-Time Testing Using ASAM XIL API TargetScripts
documents.content:
The `TargetScriptRTT` class provides the `run()` method to execute a TargetScript with automatic resource management. The below example demonstrates the minimal use case:

```
from dspace.testautomation.targetscript import TargetScriptRTT

targetscript = TargetScriptRTT(
    script_path="path/to/script.py"
)
targetscript.run(timeout=10)
```

What happens automatically

During initialization:

The `TargetScriptRTT` class identifies the target platform via the provided `port` parameter or uses the first available port that supports the TargetScriptCapability if none is specified. If more than one port is available, an exception is raised, as you must explicitly specify which port to use.

The `application_part` parameter is used to specify the application part on the target platform where the real-time script should be loaded. It is only required when working with multiprocessor or multicore systems. If you do not provide it, the first task name of the target MAPort is used by default
documents.title: Simple Execution

breadcrumbs: Real-Time Testing Using ASAM XIL API TargetScripts
documents.content:
the real-time script should be loaded. It is only required when working with multiprocessor or multicore systems. If you do not provide it, the first task name of the target MAPort is used by default to derive the application part name.

A TargetScript description is generated with all parameters and search paths provided, if any. This description is used to create a TargetScript instance on the XIL API server.

During `run()`:

The real-time script is loaded and started on the target platform using the XIL API. Then the script completion is awaited, and cleanup is performed automatically. This is a blocking operation. If the script stops unexpectedly with an error, a `RuntimeError` is raised with detailed error information.

If the script finished successfully, the `run()` method returns a dictionary containing the script's output parameters and their values.

ℹ️ Important: The system waits for the script to reach a completed state. If the script does not complete within the time

documents.content:
urns a dictionary containing the script's output parameters and their values.

ℹ️ Important: The system waits for the script to reach a completed state. If the script does not complete within the time specified by the `timeout` argument, a `TimeoutError` is raised. The default timeout is 10 seconds. To wait indefinitely, set `timeout` to -1.

⚠️ Warning: The object instantiation allocates resources that require cleanup. These resources are disposed at the end of the `run()` call. If additional code between the object instantiation and `run()` has the possibility of raising an exception, ensure proper cleanup by calling the `release()` method in case of an exception, e.g.,

```
targetscript = TargetScriptRTT(
    script_path="path/to/script.py"
)
try:
    function_that_may_raise(targetscript)
    output_parameters = targetscript.run()
finally:
    targetscript.release()
```

documents.content:
For finer control over test phases, transition the TargetScript's states manually. The general execution order is

- `TargetScriptRTT` instantiation to initialize the instance. Create a TargetScript object from generated dSPACE TargetScript configuration XML.
- `load()` to download the script to the target.
- `start()` to start the real-time script.
- `wait_for_sequence_end()` to wait for script completion.
- `release()` to free all allocated resources.

```
targetscript = TargetScriptRTT(
    script_path="path/to/script.py",
    port=my_port,
    application_part="Processor1",
    load_parameters={"Mapping": "{'var1': 'path1'}"},
    start_parameters={"param": 100},
    output_parameters={"Testverdict": 0},
    search_paths=["additional/path"]
)

# Manual control over each phase
try:
    targetscript.load()
    targetscript.start()
    targetscript.wait_for_sequence_end()

    targetscript.start(                     # Rerun the script with different arguments,
documents.title: Explicit Load, Start, and Cleanup

documents.content:
ver each phase
try:
    targetscript.load()
    targetscript.start()
    targetscript.wait_for_sequence_end()

    targetscript.start(                     # Rerun the script with different arguments,
        start_parameters={"param": 200})    # no need to reload

    targetscript.wait_for_sequence_end(timeout=8)
finally:

```

This approach allows you to load the script once and run it multiple times without having to reload between runs, which saves time in test execution.

ℹ️ Important: `wait_for_sequence_end()` is a blocking call that waits for the script to reach a completed state. If the script does not complete within the time specified by the `timeout` argument, a `TimeoutError` is raised. The default timeout is 10 seconds. To wait indefinitely, set `timeout` to -1.

breadcrumbs: Real-Time Testing Using ASAM XIL API TargetScripts
documents.content:
The TargetScriptRTT class provides a property to get the current state of the real-time script running on the target platform. The possible states are:

- `IN_CONFIGURATION`: The real-time script has not been loaded to the target platform. This is the initial state after creation of a TargetScript object or after the real-time script has been removed from the target system.
- `READY`: The real-time script has been loaded to the target platform and is ready to run. This state is reached after calling `load()`.
- `RUNNING`: The real-time script is executing. This state is reached after calling `start()`.
- `FINISHED`: The real-time script execution has been successfully completed. Values of the script's output parameters (if available) can be retrieved.
- `STOPPED`: The real-time script execution has been stopped, e.g., due to a run-time error or due to a client request via `stop()`. Output parameter values are not available.
- `PAUSED`: The real-time script execution is interrupted,
documents.title: TargetScript States

breadcrumbs: Real-Time Testing Using ASAM XIL API TargetScripts
documents.content:
execution has been stopped, e.g., due to a run-time error or due to a client request via `stop()`. Output parameter values are not available.
- `PAUSED`: The real-time script execution is interrupted, but can be resumed from the point of interruption, as the execution status is preserved. This state can be reached by calling the `pause()` method and can be resumed by invoking `start()`.
- `RELEASED`: The XIL API TargetScript object is released.

Note that state may change immediately after retrieval. This is particularly relevant when the script is in the `RUNNING` state, as it may finish and transition to `STOPPED` or `FINISHED` at any moment. Other states require explicit actions to transition.

)

The Targetscript package includes a helper function `generate_mapping_dict()` to automatically generate variable mapping dictionaries.

dSPACE real-time testing scripts do not have access to the XIL API variable mapping active in the test environment, and therefore rely on hard-coded variable paths, which may not be ideal for flexible testing. To address this limitation, you can provide a subset of the mapping as a dictionary containing the variables used in the real-time script. The `generate_mapping_dict()` function acts as a bridge to create this mapping dictionary using the currently active mapping in the test environment on the host side.

You can send this mapping dictionary to the real-time script as load parameters. Within the real-time script, you can retrieve this dictionary from the load arguments and initialize test variables with the identifiers sent from the host side.

```
from dspace.testautomation.targetscript import (
    TargetScriptRTT, generate_mapping_dict)

#

documents.content:
A key feature of the Test Automation SDK is the ability to configure a test environment via a YAML configuration file, set it up at beginning of tests, and provide convenient access to its defined components during test execution.

This chapter explains the configuration, access patterns, and integration with pytest with a focus on the `TestEnvironmentAccess`.
documents.title: Test Environment Access

documents.content:
The entire test environment is configured in a single YAML file, which is consumed by the registry during test setup.

From the SDK’s perspective, a test environment mainly consists of two parts:

- Ports: A port is an abstraction over a third-party hardware or software resource. It features a life-cycle model and access to defined parts of the resource, e.g., model variables. For more information on configuring ports, refer to Ports – Configuration.
- Variable mappings: A mapping from unique, short alias names to port-specific variable identifiers and their associated port. Tests can be expressed against aliases, making them portable across environments by simply remapping aliases. Configuration details for variable mappings are provided in Variable Mapping — Configuration.

There are further configurations possible, e.g., to configure the used .NET Runtime. Different .NET Runtimes might be needed depending on software releases or operating systems. Information about that can be
documents.title: Test Environment Configuration

documents.content:
re further configurations possible, e.g., to configure the used .NET Runtime. Different .NET Runtimes might be needed depending on software releases or operating systems. Information about that can be found at .NET Runtime Configuration

Tip: The Test Automation SDK Python package contains a JSON schema file defining the format and possible values of the test environment YAML file. You can provide the schema file to your favorite IDE or editor, e.g., VSCode, to benefit from code completion and validation during editing.

The easiest way to obtain the schema file is the `dsta schema` command, which writes `testenv_schema.json` to a directory of your choice:

```
dsta schema --output ./schemas
```
documents.title: Test Environment Configuration

documents.content: TestEnvironmentAccess
documents.title: TestEnvironmentAccess

documents.content:
The `TestEnvironmentAccess` is a Python context manager that manages the life cycle of all ports defined in the YAML configuration file.

- Entering the context: All ports are set up according to their configured `target_state`.
- Leaving the context: All ports are stopped, disconnected, and released.

When using the SDK together with pytest, the Test Automation SDK pytest plugin exposes a session-scoped fixture named `ta`, which returns a `TestEnvironmentAccess` object. The fixture ensures the test environment is set up once per session and that all ports are released when testing finishes.
documents.title: Port lifecycle context manager

documents.content:
Ports and variable aliases are accessed through the `TestEnvironmentAccess` instance. It exposes two collections:

- `ports` – access named ports via `ta.ports["PortName"]` or `ta.ports.PortName`.
- `vars` – access variable aliases via `ta.vars["Alias"]` or `ta.vars.Alias`.

Aliases resolve to `FrameworkVariable` objects. When the value property of a framework variable is accessed, the alias is looked up in the registry, which provides the mapping information. Using this mapping, the framework determines the corresponding port-specific `PortVariable` and delegates the read or write operation to the associated port.

The variable mapping configuration contains a `type` property for the port-specific identifier ([`PortVariable`]). The Test Automation SDK uses NumPy data types for numerical data to ensure type consistency, e.g., with static typed dotnet implementation like the XIL API Ports.

Limitation: Variable access supports scalar, vector, and matrix values. Special lookup table
documents.title: Variable Access

documents.content:
cal data to ensure type consistency, e.g., with static typed dotnet implementation like the XIL API Ports.

Limitation: Variable access supports scalar, vector, and matrix values. Special lookup table values, such as Curve and Map, are not yet supported.
documents.title: Variable Access

documents.content: The registry is a central singleton object that stores port and variable mapping information for the entire test environment. It is populated during test setup and is used internally by `TestEnvironmentAccess` to resolve variable aliases to their corresponding ports.
documents.title: The Registry

In combination with pytest, accessing model variables in tests can be achieved as follows:

1. Configure the test environment

   The `mappings` section refers to an external mapping file (CSV in this example) that defines which aliases are available and how they map to ports and their port-specific identifiers. The `PortId` column in the mapping file must match the `name` of a port defined in the YAML configuration file (here: `"Model"`).

   `test-environment.yaml`:

   ```
   ports:
   - type: XIL API MAPort
       name: Model
       order: 10
       target_state: CONNECTED
       config:
           factory:
           vendor_name: dSPACE GmbH
           product_name: XIL API
           product_version: 2024-A
           port_config_file: VEOS/turnlamp/Variable Descriptions/MAPortConfig.xml
           force_config: true

   mappings:
   - file: VEOS/turnlamp/mapping.csv
     type: CSV
   ```

   `VEOS/turnlamp/mapping.csv`:

   ```
2. Write the test

   pytest discovers all tests where the function name starts with the `test_` prefix. The `ta` fixture is provided by the Test Automation SDK pytest plug-in. It is session-scoped and returns a ready-to-use `TestEnvironmentAccess` instance.

   ```
   from dspace.testautomation import Capturing, TestEnvironmentAccess

   def test_turnlamp(ta: TestEnvironmentAccess) -> None:
       # arrange: write initial values

ronmentAccess` instance.

   ```
   from dspace.testautomation import Capturing, TestEnvironmentAccess

   def test_turnlamp(ta: TestEnvironmentAccess) -> None:
       # arrange: write initial values
       ta.vars.BatteryVoltage.value = 12 # Voltage in Volts
       ta.vars.TurnSignalLever.value = 0 # off

       # act: switch the turn signal lever to right, while capturing turn lamps for left and right
       with Capturing([ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft, ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight]) as capt:
         ta.vars.TurnSignalLever.value = 1 # right
         time.sleep(2) # Avoid using `time.sleep()` in production tests; it is included here for simplicity.

       # assert: turn lamps for left are always equal to zero (no flashing) and
       #   turn lamps for right are at least sometimes equal to one (lights on).
       assert capt[ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft].eq(0).all()
       assert capt[ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight].eq(1).any()
   ```

       assert capt[ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight].eq(1).any()
   ```

   Note the usage of `ta.vars.BatteryVoltage.value = 12` to set the `BatteryVoltage`, which writes the value of `12` to the model variable `Model Root/BatteryVoltage[V]/Value` of the associated XIL API MAPort named `Model`.

   Furthermore the `FrameworkVariable` returned by `ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft` is used to reference the corresponding model variable to be captured.
3. Execute the tests

   To execute tests with pytest and the Test Automation SDK, specify the YAML configuration file via a pytest argument provided by the plug-in. The registry is populated from this configuration, and the session-scoped `ta` fixture uses `TestEnvironmentAccess` as a context manager to set up and tear down the environment.

   ```
   pytest . --testenv-config=test-environment.yaml
   ```

   Alternative: You can

   pytest . --testenv-config=test-environment.yaml

   Alternative: You can configure the test environment path in a `pytest.ini` file to avoid specifying it on every command:

   ```
   [pytest]
   testenv_config = test-environment.yaml
   ```

   With this configuration, you can run tests with a simpler command:

   ```
   pytest .
   ```

   The command-line argument `--testenv-config` takes precedence over the ini option if both are provided.

The SCBT demo is available as an addition to the dSPACE Test Automation SDK. To access the demo, please contact your dSPACE representative.

The SCBT demo uses the ASM Traffic model, which extends the ASM Vehicle Dynamics model. The ASM Vehicle Dynamics model simulates the dynamics of a passenger car which includes the vehicle's longitudinal, lateral, and vertical dynamics. Furthermore, it includes an environment model which is divided into maneuver, road, and traffic components. With ASM Traffic, you can additionally simulate the movement of fellow vehicles as well as several sensor models equipped to the ASM vehicle.

The demo tests showcase:

- Dynamic scenario execution with flexible parameterization.
- Advanced signal capturing with trigger-based recording.
- Safety validations including collision detection and time-to-collision (TTC) checks.
- Integrated reporting with signal plots for analysis.

These tests provide a practical example of how the SDK supports scalable and

documents.content: The TurnSignal tests verify one shared set of functional scenarios. They cover left and right turn signaling, warning light behavior, reaction times, and robust lever handling. The goal is to validate the expected TurnSignal behavior consistently across the demo.
documents.title: Test scenarios

documents.content:
The shared TurnSignal scenarios are available in two complementary implementations:

- `tests/test_turnsignaltests.py`: Post-processes measured signal data after Python-driven stimulation.
- `tests/test_turnsignaltests_targetscript.py`: Executes the same scenario family through RTT with RTT observers and checks.

Both suites are intended to stay aligned in scenario intent and pass or fail semantics. This overlap is deliberate so the demo keeps the focus on the TurnSignal tests themselves while also showing two execution styles in the same SDK-driven environment.
documents.title: Implementation note

documents.content:
The scenario identifiers T010 through T070 define the shared functional checks used by both approaches. In the capture-based suite, these scenarios are parameterized over 7 battery voltages: 7.0 V, 7.5 V, 8.0 V, 11.0 V, 14.0 V, 14.5 V, and 15.0 V.

Scenario Purpose Expected outcome T010 Turn signal left Left front and rear signals flash, while the right side stays inactive. T020 Turn signal right Right front and rear signals flash, while the left side stays inactive. T030 Warning light All four turn signals and the warning light indicator flash while the warning light is active. T040 Warning light together with turn signal Warning light behavior keeps priority even while the lever is cycled through LEFT, RIGHT, and OFF. T050 Reaction time of turn signals The commanded-side turn signals react to lever input in less than 100 ms. T060 Reaction time of the warning light switch All turn signals and the warning light indicator react to warning-light activation in less than 50 ms. T070
documents.title: Shared scenario set: T010 to T070

documents.content:
als react to lever input in less than 100 ms. T060 Reaction time of the warning light switch All turn signals and the warning light indicator react to warning-light activation in less than 50 ms. T070 Monkey test for turn-signal lever Pulses stay within 450 ms to 550 ms, front and rear signals stay synchronized per side, and left and right are never active at the same time.

In the RTT suite, the corresponding checks are expressed through RTT observers and checks such as O010, O020, O030, and O040. In the capture-based suite, the same acceptance criteria are evaluated on the recorded signals after the stimulation sequence has finished.
documents.title: Shared scenario set: T010 to T070

documents.content:
The RTT suite in `tests/test_turnsignaltests_targetscript.py` extends beyond the shared T010 to T070 scenario set. It also includes additional RTT-oriented sequences, including replay-based cases that load recorded inputs into RTT.

To make these RTT sequences portable across supported demo environments, the Python test transfers an explicit variable mapping into RTT. This avoids hard-coded signal paths and lets the RTT scripts resolve the variables from the active Test Automation SDK test environment.
documents.title: RTT-specific notes

documents.content:
Besides the scenario-oriented TurnSignal suites, the demo folder also contains smaller modules that focus on specific SDK capabilities:

- `tests/test_demo_capturing_focused.py`: Examples centered on capturing workflows. This includes triggered captures, MF4 recording, `MultiPortCapturing`, and direct control over the capture lifecycle.
- `tests/test_demo_rtt_focused.py`: Standalone `TargetScriptRTT` examples. This includes data replay from a file and fine-grained script control.
- `tests/test_demo_failure_simulation.py`: Electrical error simulation examples for environments that provide the required error-configuration support.

Create a new file, for example: `tests/test_turnlamp_activation.py`.

1. Import the required packages:

   import time

   def test_turnlamp_activation(ta: TestEnvironmentAccess):

   ```
   def test_turnlamp_activation(ta: TestEnvironmentAccess):
       # Arrange
       # Set battery voltage
       ta.vars.BatteryVoltage.value = 12.0

       # Ensure lever is turned OFF
       ta.vars.TurnSignalLever.value = 0
   ```

Context manager for the configuration and start/stop of a ControlDesk recorder.

Note that the recorder implements the `AbstractCapture`, but does not have any port reference, thus it will raise an exception if the port is accessed.

In addition to the `AbstractCapture` interface, it supports the context manager
documents.title: Recorder

documents.content:
s the `AbstractCapture`, but does not have any port reference, thus it will raise an exception if the port is accessed.

In addition to the `AbstractCapture` interface, it supports the context manager protocol. This allows it to be used similarly to the `Capturing` context manager.

Any method that interacts with the underlying ControlDesk automation interface may raise a `ControlDeskAutomationError`.

The `variables` parameter is optional; variables to capture can also be configured after initialization via the `variables` property.

The measurement raster may be defined by providing either a `raster_name` or a `raster_period`. The two parameters are mutually exclusive; both can be omitted.

- If `raster_name` is provided, it must be available on all measurement platforms with a consistent sampling period. `OnEvent` and `OnChange` raster types can only be selected by `raster_name`. A `CaptureError` is raised if this condition is not met.
- If `raster_period` is provided:

  - A
documents.title: Recorder

documents.content:
nsistent sampling period. `OnEvent` and `OnChange` raster types can only be selected by `raster_name`. A `CaptureError` is raised if this condition is not met.
- If `raster_period` is provided:

  - A periodical raster with a matching common period is selected. The exact requested period is preferred. If unavailable, the next shorter common period is used and a warning is logged. If no common periodical raster exists, a `CaptureError` is raised.
  - If rasters with equal sample periods and different MeasurementRasterType are available, the time-based raster is preferred over hardware-polling and polling rasters.
- If neither `raster_name` nor `raster_period` is provided, ControlDesk selects the raster individually per signal.

Although it is possible to omit the raster specification, this may lead to ControlDesk selecting the `"onChange"` raster for parameter signals, which is presumably not desired. Refer to the ControlDesk documentation for more details.

```

Set a start trigger. After `start()`, the capturing then waits for the condition to be satisfied.

The `condition` denotes the trigger condition to start the recording. It is provided as a string in ControlDesk trigger rule syntax.

Optionally, a `delay` in seconds can be specified to define a trigger delay or a pre-trigger interval. A positive value delays the actual start of the capture after the trigger condition is satisfied. A negative value defines a pre-trigger interval, meaning that the capture should start that many seconds before the trigger condition is satisfied.

set_stop_trigger(
    condition_or_duration: str | float,
    delay: float | None = None,
) -> None
```

Set a stop trigger. If a stop trigger is set, a started capture automatically ends when the condition is satisfied or the duration elapses.

The `condition_or_duration` denotes either the trigger condition to end the recording or a duration in seconds. A condition is provided as a string in ControlDesk trigger rule syntax. A duration is provided as a number in seconds.

Optionally, a `delay` in seconds can be specified to define a trigger delay. A positive value delays the actual end of the capture after the trigger condition is satisfied. A negative value is not supported.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default `condition_or_duration` `str | float`

The trigger condition when to stop recording in ControlDesk trigger rule syntax or a duration in seconds.

required `delay` `float | None`

An optional trigger delay in seconds.

`None`

Get all measured data as `pandas.DataFrame`.

Returns an empty DataFrame if no data was captured, e.g., when the start trigger was not satisfied and `require_recording=False`. The empty DataFrame has columns matching the configured signal names but no rows.

Data frames are best suited for scalar variables captured on matching timestamps. If values of different variables are captured on different timestamps, missing values may be filled by placeholder values, e.g., NaN, and data types of included time series may change to accommodate those values.

This module provides functions to: - Load a specified .NET runtime, - Load specified assemblies, - Retrieve .NET types from already loaded assemblies.

The goal is to defer loading of the .NET runtime until it can be determined from the test environment configuration YAML file. Therefore, run-time loading cannot occur at import time.

All attempts by the application to load assemblies, retrieve types, or create instances from .NET assemblies should be routed through the functions provided in this module.

Important: Do not import `pythonnet` or `clr` elsewhere in the codebase. Use only this module for .NET interop.

Copyright February 2026, dSPACE SE & Co. KG. All rights reserved.
documents.title: dotnet

documents.content:
```
ensure_runtime(
    *,
    runtime: str | None = None,
    runtime_config: str | PathLike[str] | None = None,
    dotnet_root: str | PathLike[str] | None = None,
    search_dirs: str
    | PathLike[str]
    | Sequence[str | PathLike[str]]
    | None = None,
) -> object
```

Ensure the specified .NET runtime is loaded.

Must be called BEFORE the first call to `load_assembly` or `get_type`, otherwise the default runtime may already be selected. It is safe to call `ensure_runtime` multiple times, but it is not possible to change an already loaded .NET runtime.

The specified `runtime` can be any string suitable for pythonnet. Currently these are: - "netfx" : .NET Framework. Default on Windows and only supported there. - "coreclr" : .NET Core. Default on Linux.

In case of `coreclr` a runtimeconfig.json should be provided to specify version and further options. If `runtime_config` is omitted, it is determined from `PYTHONNET_CORECLR_RUNTIME_CONFIG` environment variable if present.

An

An optional sequence of `search_dirs` can be provided. All paths are added to the python search path `sys.path` collection. Assemblies can then be found and loaded from these paths.

This module defines the scalar, vector, matrix, configuration, and variable-value aliases shared by ports, framework variables, and generated stubs. The aliases describe both the normalized numpy-based values used inside the SDK and the broader Python input shapes accepted at public boundaries.

All NumPy scalar types that can be read from and written to port-specific variables.

Covers floating-point, signed integer, unsigned integer, Boolean, and unicode string scalars. Complex numbers, byte strings, and void types are not supported.

Read values are represented as NumPy scalars or NumPy arrays to provide stable numeric semantics independent of the underlying tool or platform.

Enumeration of possible (lifecycle) states of a port.

The `AbstractPort` and its concrete subclasses wrap various third-party components of a test environment and abstracts over the creation and release lifecycle. What resources are managed by the port is implementation-specific and the `PortState` enumeration reflects stages of that lifecycle.

Instances of concrete subclasses of AbstractPort are created based on the test environment .yaml file.

RELEASED = 0
```

The wrapped port resource is not yet created or already released.

CREATED = 1
```

The wrapped port resource is created but not yet configured or connected.
documents.title: CREATED class-attribute instance-attribute

documents.content:
```
CONNECTED = 2
```

The wrapped port resource is connected. This means the wrapped port resource is fully configured, operable, and ready to use.
documents.title: CONNECTED class-attribute instance-attribute

documents.content:
```
STARTED = 3
```

The wrapped port resource is started. The meanings depends on the port, but in general `STARTED` state is considered a substate of `CONNECTED`, and might not be meaningful for all port implementations.

Enumeration that specifies the operational context under which a port lifecycle transition method is invoked.

When a ports lifecycle transition method (`create()`, `configure()`, `start()`, `stop()`, `disconnect()`, or `release()`) is triggered as part of the automated lifecycle management, this enumeration indicates whether the invocation occurs during the setup or teardown procedure. If the context argument is omitted, the method should be treated as a manual invocation outside the managed lifecycle.

The ControlDesk lifecycle `PortState` is interpreted as follows:

- `RELEASED`: The ControlDeskPort on the Test Automation SDK side is created but has not yet accessed, or has already released, any internal COM instances of the ControlDesk application.
- `CREATED`: The ControlDeskPort internally manages an instance of the ControlDesk application COM object.
- `CONNECTED`: The ControlDesk application is configured as specified according to the project and experiment. If the ControlDesk application has a different project open or a different experiment active, then the state is considered `CREATED` rather than `CONNECTED`.
- `STARTED`: The ControlDesk application has started the online calibration and is configured as specified. If the ControlDesk application is currently online but has a divergent project/experiment, the state is considered `CREATED` rather than `STARTED`.

This modules provides utility functions for the consistent logging of port lifecycle management and other (presumably long-running) port actions. The defined context managers should ony be used to log port actions.

Two context managers are defined for sophisticated logging: - `log_port_lifecycle`, to log lifecycle management actions and state transitions. - `log_port_action_debug`, to log other presumably long-runnning actions, but only at debug level.

    logger: Logger,

) -> typing.Generator[None, None, None]
```

Context manager to log common lifecycle management actions of derivates of `AbstractPort`.

This method logs first an info, consisting of the specified method and port identification. If an exception occured in the body, it is augmented (`Exception.add_note()`) with context information, and optionally logged. In the end, the completion and current state of the port are logged with debug level.

Use, e.g., as follows:

```
def create(self, **kwargs: typing.Any) -> None:
    with _logging.log_port_lifecycle(_logger, self, "create", "Get ControlDesk COM object."):
        self._controldesk = controldesk.get_application(self._prog_id)
```

Bases: `AbstractCapture`

Common intermediate implementation of XIL API captures.

Any method that interacts with the underlying XIL API testbench may raise a `XilTestbenchError`.

The measurement raster must be defined by providing either a `raster_name` or a `raster_period`. The two parameters are mutually exclusive; exactly one must be provided.

- If `raster_name` is provided, a task with this exact name is selected. Event-driven rasters can only be selected by `raster_name`. A `CaptureError` is raised if no matching task is found.
- If `raster_period` is provided, a timer-driven task with a matching period is selected. If no exact match exists, the next shorter timer-driven task is used. If the period is shorter than all available timer-driven tasks, a `CaptureError` is raised.

A negative value defines a pre-trigger interval, meaning that the capture should start that many seconds before the trigger condition is satisfied.

Real-time testing support.

This module provides the main `TargetScriptRTT` class for executing dSPACE real-time testing scripts using the ASAM XIL API TargetScripts. It includes also helper functions like `generate_mapping_dict`.

```
TargetScriptRTT(
    script_path: str | PathLike[str],

    port: str | TargetScriptCapability | None = None,

A manager for real-time testing operations.

Provides functions for loading, running, and managing dSPACE real-time testing scripts on target systems based on ASAM TargetScript.

To avoid errors due to race conditions, do not manage the same TargetScript instance concurrently, e.g., from different threads.

Initialize a dSPACE real-time script as TargetScript.

The TargetScript is created for a specific port which must support the TargetScriptCapability. If exactly one port is registered in the `Registry` that supports this capability and no port is specified, this port is used automatically. Otherwise, the
documents.title: TargetScriptRTT

documents.content:
ich must support the TargetScriptCapability. If exactly one port is registered in the `Registry` that supports this capability and no port is specified, this port is used automatically. Otherwise, the port must be specified by `port` parameter.

For multiprocessor or multicore systems, `application_part` specifies on which application part the real-time script will be executed. If the application part is not provided for MP/MC systems, the application part name is derived from the first task on the provided port.

The script parameters must be specified as `load_parameters`, `start_parameters`, and `output_parameters`. The arguments can be omitted if no parameters of that type are used in the real-time script. The script parameters are declared as dictionaries where the keys are the parameter names and the values are the initial parameter values. For dSPACE real-time scripts, the order of the parameters in the dictionaries must match the order expected by the script implementation.

Get stop information for a real-time script that is stopped.

Retrieves diagnostic information about why the script entered the STOPPED state. This is only available in STOPPED state, trying to get the stop information in any other state will raise an exception.

A `StopInfo` object is returned which is managed by the ASAM XIL API. It has the following properties:

- `Code`: ASAM standard error code.
- `CodeDescription`: Human-readable description of the ASAM error.
- `VendorCode`: Vendor-specific error code for additional diagnostics.
- `VendorCodeDescription`: Vendor-specific error information.

If the target script is not in the STOPPED state, the property yields `None`.

Context manager that creates a port-specific capture object and captures specified variables while inside the `with` block.

The raster for measuring the variable values must be defined by providing either a `raster_name` or a `raster_period`. The two parameters are mutually exclusive, but one of the parameters must be provided.

The measurement raster selection is delegated to the created port-specific capture object, and in general, the following rules apply:

- If the raster is defined by `raster_name`, a raster with this exact name is selected. Event-driven and change-driven rasters can only be selected by `raster_name`.
- If the raster is defined by `raster_period`, a periodical raster with a
documents.title: Capturing

documents.content:
ame`, a raster with this exact name is selected. Event-driven and change-driven rasters can only be selected by `raster_name`.
- If the raster is defined by `raster_period`, a periodical raster with a matching period is selected. If no exact match is found, the periodical raster with the greatest raster period lower than the specified `raster_period` must be selected.

When the context manager is created, it creates a port-specific capture object if all specified variables are resolved to the same port. If more than one port is addressed by specified variables, a `CaptureError` is raised. You may want to use a `MultiPortCapture` in that case, but MultiPortCapture has its own drawbacks and limitations.

When entering the context, the port-specific capture object is started, by invoking `start()` on it, and the port-specific capture is returned as a context value that can be bound to a variable by the `as` clause. If any exception occurs during the start, the port-specific capture

ng `start()` on it, and the port-specific capture is returned as a context value that can be bound to a variable by the `as` clause. If any exception occurs during the start, the port-specific capture object is released instantly.

When leaving the context, the context manager waits for the port-specific capture to finish if a `stop_trigger` was specified. Otherwise the port-specific capture object is immediately stopped and released by invoking `stop()` and `release()` respectively.

If `start_trigger` was defined but not satisfied when leaving the context, a `CaptureError` is raised by default. This prevents captures from appearing successful when no data was actually recorded. Set `require_recording` to false to continue without captured signals instead of raising an exception. `require_recording` has no effect if no start trigger is specified.

When `require_recording=False` and the start trigger is not satisfied, the returned capture object will provide empty data: -

When `require_recording=False` and the start trigger is not satisfied, the returned capture object will provide empty data: - `get_data_frame()` returns an empty DataFrame, which has columns matching the configured signal names but no rows. - `get_signal()` and the `[]` operator return an empty pandas Series.

If any exception occurs during stopping, the port-specific capture object is released instantly.

After the context, captured signals for specified variables can be retrieved from the context value, which is the port-specific capture object returned by `__enter__` and bound by the `as` clause. Use the random access operator to get signals by name or their `FrameworkVariable`.

Example:

```
ta.vars.TurnSignalLever = 0

with Capturing(
        [ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft, ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontRight,],
        raster_period=0.01) as capture:
    sleep(1)
    ta.vars.TurnSignalLever = 1
    sleep(1)
    ta.vars.TurnSignalLever = 0

# assert that left signal is at least once flashing, contains on and off
assert (capture[ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft] == 1).any()
assert (capture[ta.vars.TurnSignalFrontLeft] == 0).any()
```

Context manager to work with an electrical error simulation (EES) configuration from file. Initializes an electrical error simulation configuration from an error configuration XML file.

This context manager is port-agnostic and works with any port supporting the `ElectricalErrorCapability`. It creates a port-specific error configuration and manages its lifecycle (download, activate, deactivate, unload).

When the context manager is created, it creates a port-specific error configuration object and connects it to the EES port. If more than one port is available, it must be specified by parameter (details see below).

When entering the context, the error configuration is downloaded and activated by invoking `download()` and then `activate()`. The error configuration is returned as a context

When entering the context, the error configuration is downloaded and activated by invoking `download()` and then `activate()`. The error configuration is returned as a context value that can be bound to a variable by the `as` clause. If any exception occurs during the start, the error configuration object is deactivated and unloaded instantly.

When leaving the context, Otherwise the error configuration object is deactivated and unloaded instantly by invoking `deactivate()` and then `unload()` respectively.

One-Factor-At-a-Time (OFAT) implementation module.

This module provides functions for generating test cases using the OFAT method, a Design of Experiments (DoE) approach where each test case varies exactly one parameter from its default value while keeping all other parameters constant.

OFAT is useful for: - Isolating the impact of individual parameters on system behavior - Identifying which parameters have the most significant effects - Debugging issues related to specific parameter changes - Creating targeted test coverage with minimal test cases

While OFAT does not capture parameter interactions like full factorial designs, it provides a good balance between test coverage and test case count.

Copyright February 2026, dSPACE SE & Co. KG. All rights reserved.

documents.title: Failing Test Execution Due to Blocked XIL API Ports

documents.content:
All Test Automation SDK tests that use XIL API fail with an execution error. Running the tests again does not resolve the issue.

Error message: `Port configuration could not be completed successfully.`
documents.title: Situation

documents.content:
When a Test Automation SDK testing session is forcefully terminated, the SDK has no opportunity to execute its registered teardown handlers. This leads to an incomplete cleanup of test resources. It might happen during debugging sessions or when the Python process is stopped. External resources (such as the XIL API) that might require an explicit release remain in an inconsistent or locked state.

When starting another test, these resources are not available and therefore the test cannot be executed. In the case of the XIL API, the ports stay blocked and cannot be used until they are released or the XIL API is shut down.
documents.title: Reason

documents.content:
Release the ports manually or shut down the XIL API.

Windows

On Windows, this can be done by navigating to the right corner of the taskbar and clicking the up arrow to Show the hidden system tray icons. In the system tray overflow window, right-click "dSPACE XIL API Server 20XX-X", recognizable by the red 'd' icon, and left-click one of the options "Release ports" or "Shutdown". After a few seconds, the icon disappears as the XIL API shuts down. You should now be able to run new tests.

Try to avoid forced termination of test automation executions. If necessary, stop them in a controlled manner, e.g., via a keyboard interrupt using `Ctrl+C`. Do not cancel or restart debugging sessions. Let the process end on its own.
documents.title: Solution
